messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 74

She still arrives at the office before nine, as she always did, but now she parks directly under the brightest light in the lot and keeps her keys threaded between her knuckles until she reaches the lobby door. Three years ago, she would have worked until midnight without a second thought. That was how she earned her reputation as the tax consultant who never missed a deadline, the one who could untangle the messiest corporate filings while the rest of the team packed up at six. She was proud of that.

The event happened on a Tuesday in early December. She had stayed late to finalize a quarterly return for a mid-size client. The office was empty by eight. When the cleaning crew came in, she barely looked up. One of them—she never learned his real name, the police said he used a false ID—waited until she went to the break room for coffee. He grabbed her from behind, pressed something sharp against her neck, and dragged her into the supply closet.

She was there for nine hours.

He made her sit on the floor with her wrists bound by zip ties and her mouth taped. He talked at her, mostly about money, about how her clients were all thieves, about how she was complicit. She did not answer. She counted the water-stained ceiling tiles to keep her mind from the knife he rested on her thigh. A janitor found her after the morning shift started. The man had left an hour earlier, simply walked out.

Her body healed quickly. The tape left a raw ring around her lips for a week; the zip ties gouged shallow red lines into her wrists. But the inside of her did not heal the same way. She took three months of leave, then went back to work because the firm sent a kind email about how they had her office cleaned and reorganized, and she thought returning would make her feel normal again.

It did not.

Now she cannot sit in her cubicle with her back to the door. She has rearranged the furniture so the entrance is always in her peripheral vision. Every footstep in the hallway makes her pause mid-keystroke. Her fingers freeze over the number pad; she forgets what she was calculating. The long December nights especially are unbearable. She leaves before sunset, making excuses to her manager about evening appointments, even though she has none.

She still prepares tax returns, but she double-checks every figure three times because she cannot trust her own concentration. A faint noise—a cough, a dropped pen—will send her mind back to the closet, back to the cold tile floor and the scratch of the man’s sleeve against her neck. She stares at her screen and sees zeros.

Her relationships have narrowed too. She used to meet colleagues for after-work drinks. Now she declines, afraid of walking to her car in the dark. She eats dinner alone in her apartment with the curtains drawn. She checks the lock on the door every few minutes. When she lies in bed, she hears the squeak of the supply closet hinge, even if the apartment is silent. She dreams of zip ties cutting into her wrists, of tape sealing her mouth, and she wakes gasping, convinced the door is about to open.

At work, she is still polite, still thorough, but her voice has gone flat. She stops herself from scanning the break room for emergency exits when she is just trying to pour coffee. She tells herself it is reasonable to be careful. But she also knows she has not had a full night’s sleep in a year, and that last week her supervisor asked if she was feeling all right because she had left a decimal error in a client’s schedule. She caught it before filing, but the mistake scared her. That was not something “careful” Lien would have made before.

She carries the weight of that Tuesday every day. She carries the closet with her into every room. And she keeps working, because she does not know what else to do, but the numbers do not settle in her mind the way they used to. They scatter, like she is still counting ceiling tiles.
